title: What If We Stopped Walking Past One Another?
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer starts from a familiar lament, that phones have replaced the casual conversation of grocery lines and airport waits, and asks what that shift means for leadership and community. Her argument is that the big problems of loneliness, housing and exhausted families lead us to dismiss the scale at which we can actually act, so walking past becomes a habit. She holds that noticing and responding to one another is a muscle that has atrophied in our individualized, screen-saturated lives. Leadership, in her framing, does not require a title or strategic plan, only the willingness to see what is within reach and participate. Small acts such as offering a ride, sharing food, making an introduction or asking a quiet colleague how they are build the connective tissue of community. She closes with reflection questions and a weekend invitation to put the phone away and choose one small act of connection.
points: Awareness of the problems we cannot fix can quietly excuse us from the ones we can, so the habit of walking past grows out of overwhelm at scale.
Noticing, asking, offering and accepting help are skills that weaken when attention is perpetually redirected to a screen.
Schafer redefines leadership as recognizing something within reach that could be made a little better and choosing to participate, no title required.
Small, undocumented exchanges build trust and the connective tissue of community, and rehearse the awareness and responsiveness larger stakes will demand.
Connection is two-way, so leaders should be curious about what others can offer them and allow themselves to need one another.
quotes: When our attention is continually sent somewhere else, we do not only lose casual conversation. We become less practiced at noticing one another.
If I cannot solve loneliness, it is easy to decide there is nothing meaningful I can do about it.

Leadership does not always require a strategic plan, a title, or even a particularly bold action. Sometimes it is simply recognizing that something within your reach could be made a little better and choosing to participate.
We have become so accustomed to associating impact with scale that we can overlook how much of a good life is created through thousands of exchanges that no one will ever document.
Those small interactions do more than brighten someone’s day. They create the connective tissue of community.
Connection, after all, is not a one-way act of generosity. Some of the most beautiful moments occur when we allow ourselves to need one another.
Which brings me back to a question I want to sit with this weekend: What have we learned to walk past simply because it has become familiar?
